messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Carlos, a 25-year-old North American man who worked as a housekeeper in a downtown hotel, came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly unable to keep his life ordered around shifts that started before dawn and ended late at night. He had grown up with a caregiver whose abuse was unpredictable and humiliating, and the memories that now tormented him were tied to a childhood night when he had been awakened in the dark, pinned by the frightening feel of a rough fabric against his skin, while a child’s crying from the next room made the whole house seem alive with threat. In the present, the same sorts of moments could seize him without warning: when he woke in his apartment before sunrise and the room was still black, when his hand brushed a particular coarse hotel towel, or when he heard children crying in the hallway outside the lobby or in the courtyard behind the building. Carlos had come to believe that other people could somehow see what had happened to him just by looking at him, and that belief made those moments feel exposing and dangerous; if he seemed marked, he reasoned, it was safer not to let anyone get too close.

At those times, the old scenes returned with overwhelming force. He described them as a film that played over and over, and when the memory came back it did not feel like a recollection but like the event itself, complete across sight, sound, touch, and the sickening sensation in his body. The feeling would hit so hard that he had to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes standing frozen in a supply closet or at the end of a hallway until he could catch his breath. Those episodes often arrived after a trigger, but they also made the triggers sharper: once the memory took over, nighttime felt more menacing, the texture of certain linens became intolerable, and a child crying nearby could instantly pull him back into the old fear. He became superalert in the hotel, scanning corridors and listening for sounds that reminded him of the past, and the more he watched for danger, the more he noticed the very cues that set him off.

Carlos’s attempts to stay safe began to organize his life around avoidance. When the dark of night or waking in darkness brought on the memories, he would drop responsibilities he knew mattered, volunteering to switch shifts, skipping errands, or putting off bills and calls so he would not have to move alone through the building before daylight. In the evenings he would drift off into a world of his own, staring at his phone or losing himself in imagined scenes until hours passed, and he made a point of never being alone with another person, preferring to stay near coworkers, houseguests, or anyone else in sight. Those strategies brought brief relief, but they also kept the traumatic material close. The more he organized his days around escape and safety, the more time he spent quietly turning the event over in his mind, and the memory stayed primed to return with the same unbearable vividness. He noticed too that these habits seemed to confirm the worst things he believed about himself: that he was not really a person to others, but something damaged and exposed, someone who had to hide because if people got a clear look they would know.

Over time, the fear of harm hardened into a general rule about people. Carlos came to feel that you could never know who would hurt you, and that conviction kept him watching everyone around him with suspicion. In the hotel, a child crying in a hallway could tighten his chest and make his skin crawl; in his apartment, a dark room at 3 a.m. could have him wide awake and listening for footsteps; a rough towel in housekeeping could stop him cold long enough for the memory to rush back. Each episode made him pull further away, and each act of withdrawing seemed to leave him more convinced that danger was everywhere and that he was somehow already singled out. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the constant guard he kept over himself, troubled that his work was suffering because he avoided tasks and lingered in distraction, and frightened that the cycle would never loosen. What finally brought him in was the realization that he could not keep building his life around darkness, textures, and crying children without losing more of it, and he hoped, more than anything, to feel like a person again rather than an object waiting for harm.
